---
title: "TypeScript Engine Extensions on Node"
---

Quarto 2 runs TypeScript execution-engine extensions (for example the
marimo and Julia engines) in a **Node.js** subprocess. Quarto 1 ran them
under its bundled Deno. This page covers what you need installed, and how
to move an engine extension that still uses the `Deno` namespace.

## What you need installed

Quarto 2 needs **Node.js 24 or newer** when a project uses a TypeScript
engine extension. Projects that use only the built-in engines never start
Node.

Quarto looks for Node in this order:

1. The `QUARTO_NODE` environment variable (a full path to a `node`
   binary). A binary that is too old is an error, not a fall-through.
2. `node` on `PATH`.
3. Well-known install locations, including Homebrew, volta, fnm, nvm and
   Windows `Program Files`.

The same variable and search order apply to `q2 mcp` and to the project
scripts that run with `node`.

## Why you may see "Deno is not defined"

An engine bundle that calls `Deno.*` fails under Node with a message like:

```
engine extension /path/to/engine.js uses the `Deno` namespace, which q2
does not provide: q2 runs TypeScript engines under Node. ...
```

Quarto does not provide a `Deno` shim. The fix belongs in the extension:
replace `Deno.*` with `node:` built-ins, then rebuild the bundle.

## `Deno` to `node:` equivalents

| Deno | Node |
|---|---|
| `Deno.readTextFileSync(p)` | `fs.readFileSync(p, "utf8")` |
| `Deno.writeTextFileSync(p, s)` | `fs.writeFileSync(p, s)` |
| `Deno.makeTempFileSync({ suffix })` | `fs.mkdtempSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), "x-"))`, then a file name with your suffix inside it |
| `Deno.stat` / `exists()` | `fs.statSync` / `fs.existsSync` |
| `Deno.env.get("X")` | `process.env.X` |
| `Deno.build.os === "windows"` | `process.platform === "win32"` |
| `Deno.exit(n)` | `process.exitCode = n` and return; avoid `process.exit` after large writes, which can truncate piped output |
| `Deno.stdout.writeSync(bytes)` | `process.stdout.write(bytes)` |
| `Deno.consoleSize()` | `process.stdout.columns` (may be `undefined`) |
| `Deno.kill(pid, sig)` | `process.kill(pid, sig)` |
| `new Deno.Command(cmd, opts)` | `child_process.spawn` / `spawnSync` (see the environment note below) |
| `crypto.subtle` + `encodeBase64` | `node:crypto` (`createHmac`) and `Buffer` |
| `jsr:@std/path`, `jsr:@std/fs` | `node:path`, `node:fs` |
| `delay(ms)` from `@std/async` | `setTimeout` from `node:timers/promises` |

Import the built-ins explicitly (`import process from "node:process"`,
`import { Buffer } from "node:buffer"`).

::: {.callout-warning}
## Environment variables are replaced, not merged

`Deno.Command` merges the `env` you pass into the parent environment.
`child_process.spawn` **replaces** it. When you set a variable for a
child, pass `env: { ...process.env, MY_VAR: "…" }`.
:::

## Keeping one bundle for both Quarto 1 and Quarto 2

Quarto 1 still runs engine extensions under Deno 2. An engine that uses
only `node:` built-ins runs unchanged on both, because Deno 2 implements
them. So the recommended port is to move to `node:` APIs and keep a single
bundle:

- Do not reference a global `Deno` anywhere in the shipped bundle; grep the
  *built* bundle, not just your sources.
- Write tests with `node:test` and `node:assert/strict`. The same files run
  under `node --test` and `deno test --no-check -A`, which gives you a Quarto 1
  check in CI.
- If your extension needs a Quarto version that supports static engine
  declarations (`name`, `claims`, `file-extensions`, `claims-files` in
  `_extension.yml`), say so with `quarto-required` in `_extension.yml`.

## Building the bundle

Build with `q2 call build-ts-extension` from the extension directory. It
bundles with rollup (embedded in `q2`, run under the same Node 24 that runs
the engine) into ESM for Node 24; it needs no Deno, no `npx` and no network.
TypeScript types are erased (not type-checked), so an import of a type must be
`import type`. Imports that only exist under Deno (`jsr:`, `npm:` specifiers
and `@std/*`) are not resolved; the build fails and names the `node:`
replacement.

If you build with your own tooling, use any bundler (esbuild, rollup, ...) with
`platform: "node"`, `format: "esm"` and `external: ["node:*"]`, and pin the
bundler version so the committed bytes are reproducible.
